native_result.query: How does incarceration affect the wealth of black individuals based on their income levels?
native_result.HypoA: The negative impact of incarceration on wealth for black individuals may be less for the high-income group than those at lower wealth ranges.
native_result.HypoB: Among Black NLSY79 respondents, having been jailed (ever_jailed = 1 during 1985-1994) is associated with markedly lower and, crucially, stagnant wealth, and the size of that wealth penalty depends on pre-incarceration economic position - though because no income variable exists in this NLSY extract, pre-incarceration wealth (composite_wealth_1985 terciles) is used as a proxy for 'income level' and is not a measured income construct. Restricting inference to Black males (race = 'black', sex = 'male'; n = 1,465, of whom 143 = 9.76% were ever jailed; Black females, 16 ever jailed at a 1.0% jail rate, are reported descriptively only and excluded from inference because the 9.8%-vs-1.0% rate difference is a confound, not extra power), ever_jailed is associated with composite_wealth_1996 averaging $11,164 versus $55,544 for never-jailed Black men (gap -$44,380, bootstrap 95% CI -$57,131 to -$32,294; -$33,143 after 1/99 winsorizing; medians $0 vs $5,450; Mann-Whitney p = 9.4e-11). The association widens monotonically across the three waves on a scale-free, inflation-immune measure - jailed/non-jailed mean wealth of 0.575 for composite_wealth_1985, 0.538 for composite_wealth_1990, and 0.201 for composite_wealth_1996 - and the process visible in the data is progressive failure to accumulate rather than a one-time level drop: from the mid-window year to the post-window year the jailed group's wealth is flat (winsorized +$578) while never-jailed Black men gained +$16,794 (difference in change -$16,143, CI -$25,499 to -$7,329). Only ~11% of the 1996 gap pre-existed in 1985 (-$4,853, CI -$8,342 to -$1,103), so ~89% accumulated during and after the jail window, and the level and change framings agree. Stratified by the income proxy, the dollar penalty rises steeply with baseline resources - T1 (1985 wealth <= $0; 63 jailed/518 not): -$19,408, ratio 0.276; T2 ($0-$5,000; 42/363): -$26,921, ratio 0.302; T3 (>$5,000; 38/441): -$86,395, ratio 0.164 - but this gradient is an estimated moderation only on the dollar scale (ever_jailed x T3 interaction = -$48,090, SE 9,754, p < 1e-6; joint tier x jail F = 12.70, p < 1e-5), whereas on the proportional scale the penalty is large and highly significant at every tier (inverse-hyperbolic-sine 1996 wealth -1.15, SE 0.25, p = 4e-06) yet not tier-dependent (joint p = 0.489; rank-percentile model p = 0.346); the honest reading is that jail is associated with a roughly constant proportional wealth penalty of about four-to-five-fold at all baseline resource levels, which mechanically yields the largest absolute dollar loss among the higher-resource Black men. Direction and tier ordering survive 1/99 winsorizing, median-, rank- and IHS-based summaries, and dropping the five largest wealth observations; all statements are associations, not causal effects, since ever_jailed is self-selected (jail rate 12-16% in the lowest baseline-wealth deciles vs 6.8% in the top).
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Inventory: confirmed 12,013 x 6 with zero missing values and NO income/education/occupation/AFQT/age/geography field, so 'income level' was operationalized as baseline composite_wealth_1985 terciles (documented as an approximation). 2) Sample restriction: inferential sample = Black males (n=1,465; 143 ever_jailed); Black females (16 jailed) descriptive only; no de-duplication, no external data, no geography design. 3) Skew handling: raw means, 1/99 winsorized means (pooled Black-male percentiles applied identically to both groups), medians/IQRs, and asinh(w/1000) IHS transforms, plus Mann-Whitney U tests and 5,000-draw bootstrap CIs. 4) Stratification: terciles (cutpoints $0 and $5,000) with treated/control counts reported alongside every stratified number, plus a <0/=/>0 split to test the zero-tie mass. 5) Pre/post framing: 1985 baseline / 1990 mid-window / 1996 post-window levels, 1985->1996 change, and the 1990->1996 segment, with the level gap decomposed into baseline gap + change gap. 6) Moderation: one pooled baseline-tier x ever_jailed interaction per scale (IHS levels, IHS change, winsorized dollars levels, winsorized dollars change, wealth rank percentile), baseline wealth controlled, HC1 robust SEs, joint F-test of the two interaction terms. 7) Inflation robustness: jailed/non-jailed wealth RATIOS per year (scale-free) as the basis of the widening claim. 8) Descriptive selection check across race x sex, explicitly not a causal DiD. Findings implemented in analysis/main_analysis.py, analysis/addendum.py, analysis/final_summary.py, consolidated in analysis/out/FINAL_REPORT.md with tables in analysis/out/*.csv.

sub_hypo.text: The negative impact of incarceration on wealth for black individuals may be less for the high-income group than those at lower wealth ranges.
sub_hypo.context: Black individuals, comparing the high-income group with those at lower wealth ranges.
sub_hypo.relations: Incarceration may have a weaker negative impact on wealth in the high-income group than among individuals at lower wealth ranges.

gold_sub_hypo.full_hypo: The negative impact of incarceration on wealth for black individuals may be less for the high-income group than those at lower wealth ranges.

sub_hypo.text: Among Black male NLSY79 respondents, having been jailed during 1985–1994 is associated with substantially lower wealth in 1996.
sub_hypo.context: Black male NLSY79 respondents (race = 'black', sex = 'male'; n = 1,465, including 143 ever jailed). Black females are descriptive only and excluded from inference.
sub_hypo.relations: Mean 1996 wealth is $11,164 for ever-jailed versus $55,544 for never-jailed men: a -$44,380 gap (bootstrap 95% CI -$57,131 to -$32,294). The winsorized gap is -$33,143; medians are $0 versus $5,450 (Mann-Whitney p = 9.4e-11). These are associations, not causal effects.

sub_hypo.text: Among Black men, the relative wealth disadvantage associated with jail widens monotonically across 1985, 1990, and 1996, reflecting progressive failure to accumulate wealth rather than merely a one-time level drop.
sub_hypo.context: Black male NLSY79 inferential sample; 1985 baseline, 1990 mid-window, and 1996 post-window relative to the 1985–1994 jail window.
sub_hypo.relations: Jailed/non-jailed mean wealth ratios decline from 0.575 in 1985 to 0.538 in 1990 and 0.201 in 1996, providing the scale-free basis for widening. From 1990 to 1996, jailed men's winsorized wealth is approximately flat (+$578), versus +$16,794 for never-jailed men; the reported difference in change is -$16,143 (95% CI -$25,499 to -$7,329). The 1985 gap is -$4,853 (95% CI -$8,342 to -$1,103), approximately 11% of the 1996 gap, with approximately 89% accumulating during and after the jail window.

sub_hypo.text: The absolute dollar wealth penalty associated with jail increases steeply with baseline wealth among Black men.
sub_hypo.context: Black male NLSY79 respondents stratified by 1985 wealth: T1 <= $0 (63 jailed/518 never jailed), T2 > $0 to $5,000 (42/363), and T3 > $5,000 (38/441). Baseline wealth terciles approximate 'income level'; income is not measured in this extract.
sub_hypo.relations: The 1996 jailed-minus-never-jailed dollar gaps are -$19,408 in T1, -$26,921 in T2, and -$86,395 in T3. Dollar-scale moderation is supported by an ever_jailed × T3 interaction of -$48,090 (SE $9,754, p < 1e-6) and joint tier × jail F = 12.70 (p < 1e-5), with baseline wealth controlled and HC1 robust SEs. Direction and dollar-tier ordering survive robustness checks including 1/99 winsorizing and dropping the five largest wealth observations.

sub_hypo.text: Despite larger absolute dollar gaps at higher baseline wealth, the proportional wealth penalty associated with jail is approximately constant across baseline resource levels among Black men.
sub_hypo.context: Black male NLSY79 respondents grouped by 1985 wealth terciles with cutpoints $0 and $5,000; these are wealth-based proxies, not measured income groups.
sub_hypo.relations: Jailed/non-jailed 1996 mean wealth ratios are 0.276, 0.302, and 0.164 in T1, T2, and T3. The hypothesis interprets the association as a roughly four-to-five-fold proportional penalty across resource levels, mechanically producing larger dollar losses at higher resources. The IHS wealth association is -1.15 (SE 0.25, p = 4e-06), but tier dependence is unsupported on IHS (joint p = 0.489) and rank-percentile (p = 0.346) scales. Median-, rank-, and IHS-based summaries support the negative association.

sub_hypo.text: Jail status is associated with baseline economic position, limiting causal interpretation of subsequent wealth differences.
sub_hypo.context: Black male NLSY79 respondents; descriptive selection check using 1985 baseline wealth deciles and jail status during 1985–1994.
sub_hypo.relations: Jail rates are 12–16% in the lowest baseline-wealth deciles versus 6.8% in the highest decile. Jail status is self-selected; wealth-level, change, and moderation findings are associations rather than causal effects or a causal difference-in-differences analysis.

sub_hypo.text: Among Black NLSY79 respondents, jail prevalence differs substantially by sex, so Black females are reported descriptively rather than pooled into wealth inference.
sub_hypo.context: Black NLSY79 respondents; race × sex descriptive selection check. Inferential wealth analyses are restricted to Black males.
sub_hypo.relations: 143 of 1,465 Black males were ever jailed (9.76%, approximately 9.8%), versus 16 Black females at a 1.0% jail rate. The hypothesis treats this sex difference as a confound, not additional inferential power.
